A single account in the club's chart of accounts. Stored as a strongly-typed Marten document
(not a barakoCMS content type) so money-adjacent code works with real Decimal
values and Marten can aggregate balances in SQL.
            
A member's receivable is modelled as a child account whose ParentCode points at
the "Accounts Receivable - Members" control account (e.g. code "1100-3322657", parent "1100"),
with MemberId linking back to the member content item.

The five classical account classes. Normal balance side is derived from this:
Asset and Expense are debit-normal; Liability, Equity and Income are credit-normal.

BarakoCMSFeaturesCollectionsRunCollectio.description: What one run did, for the operator who pressed the button.

fieldMap.description: Content field name to the dotted source path it reads.

gaps.description: Per section, what is stored and could not be exported.

document.description: A configuration document, as GET /api/config/export returns one.

requestHeaders.description:

under a name that does not read as a credential is stored with its value, and reading a

BarakoCMSFeaturesConnectorsConnectorResp.description: A connector as the API describes it.

type, so they are named instead of guessed. Empty for most callers.

post.description:
Gated by the same tenant sign-in method as codes (otp), since both prove the mailbox.
Rate limited by the same "auth" policy as the code request.
post.summary:

Always answers 200 with the same message so callers cannot probe which emails exist.

POST /api/auth/mfa/disable — turn off MFA for the signed-in user. Requires a current TOTP or a
recovery code, so a hijacked session (without the second factor) cannot remove it.

POST /api/auth/mfa/enable — confirm a pending enrollment with a code from the authenticator app.
On success MFA becomes required at login and one-time recovery codes are returned once.

POST /api/auth/mfa/setup — begin TOTP enrollment for the signed-in user. Returns a fresh secret and
otpauth URI to display once. Enrollment is not active until confirmed via /enable, so calling this

post.summary:
POST /api/auth/mfa/step-up: trade a fresh TOTP or recovery code for a short-lived step-up token.
Wrong codes count toward the same lockout as password and MFA login failures.

POST /api/auth/mfa/verify — complete a two-step login. Takes the challenge token issued by
/api/auth/login (RequiresMfa) plus a TOTP or recovery code, and on success returns the same JWT +
refresh token password login issues. Wrong codes count toward the same lockout as password failures,
so the 6-digit space can't be brute-forced.

get.summary:
GET /api/auth/oidc/{name}/callback. Where a provider redirects back to, with the code and state
in the query.

post.description:
Only for those providers: for any other this route does not exist. The state is checked exactly
as on the GET. The body is read only as a URL-encoded form of at most
MaxFormBytes, and a field sent twice counts as missing. Apple also posts an
id_token, which is ignored: the one that is validated is the one the code exchange returns.
post.summary:
POST /api/auth/oidc/{name}/callback. Where a provider configured with ResponseMode
form_post (Apple) posts the code and state back, as a form.

post.description:
Off unless the provider lists IdTokenAudiences: a native app's client id is not the web
one, and Google's native tokens name the server's client as aud and the app's as
azp. The token is checked as the callback checks it (issuer, signature against the
issuer's keys, audience, expiry, nonce, email_verified), with the configured audiences in
place of the client id.
The nonce is required, and is what makes a token usable once. Nothing ties the token to this
caller the way the state cookie ties a redirect to a browser, so a token that leaks from the app
could otherwise be exchanged by whoever has it for as long as it lives. A nonce is recorded when
it is accepted and refused again until the token it came in has expired. The record commits with
the sign-in, so a sign-in that fails leaves the token usable for a retry, and it is a unique
insert, so two requests racing with one token get one sign-in. A token whose expiry is more than
MaxTokenLifetime away is refused, which bounds how long a record is kept.
post.summary:
POST /api/auth/oidc/{name}/id-token. A native app that already holds an id token from the
provider's own SDK exchanges it for a barako token, with no browser redirect.

get.description:
Three secrets are minted and left in one HttpOnly cookie: the state that ties the callback
to this browser, the nonce that ties the id token to this request, and the PKCE verifier
that ties the code exchange to it. The provider is sent the first two and only a hash of the
third. The redirect_uri is built from the configured base URL and the configured provider
name, and nothing in the request can change where the browser is sent back to.
get.summary:
GET /api/auth/oidc/{name}/start?club={handle}. Sends the browser to the provider configured
under Oidc:Providers:{name}.

post.description:
A tenant that does not allow sign-in codes answers 403 to everybody, before any address is read.
The code a password sign-in sends to approve a new device does not come through here, so it
still works on such a tenant.
post.summary:
POST /api/auth/otp/request — email a 6-digit sign-in code to a registered user.
Always responds 200 with the same message so callers can't probe which emails exist.

POST /api/auth/otp/verify — exchange a valid email code for the same JWT + refresh token that
password login issues. Single-use, expiry-checked, with a per-code attempt cap.

get.summary: GET /api/auth/providers — which social sign-in buttons the client should show (those configured).

post.description:
The account appears at /api/auth/register/verify, when the address named here hands back
the token that was emailed to it. Until then there is no user document, so there is nothing to
sign in to, nothing holding the username, and nothing for an external provider to match against.
The third of those is why this is a security fix rather than a spam control. External sign-in
joins a provider's verified email to a local account by address alone (see
SocialSignIn.IssueAsync, which refuses any provider that has not asserted the address is
verified). Writing an arbitrary unproven address into User.Email undid that from the other
side: register as somebody else's address, wait for them to sign in with Google, and the provider
puts them into the account you control. Refusing to sign in until verified would not have closed
it, because that path never checks a password or a flag on the way in. Only the absence of the
row closes it. See DECISIONS.md D10.
Everything below answers identically whether or not the address is already registered. The one
difference a caller can see is the password policy, which is about their own input and discloses
nothing about anybody else.
The resolved tenant's sign-up policy is read first (SignUpPolicy).
A tenant that takes no sign-ups answers 403 to everybody, which says something about the tenant
and nothing about any address. An Open tenant's registration joins it with the policy's role and
gets no global role; anywhere else the account gets the global User role, as before.
post.summary: POST /api/auth/register. It asks for an account; it does not create one.

post.description:
Every rejection uses one message. A token that never existed, one that expired, one already
spent, one whose username was taken by somebody else in the meantime, and one that lost a race
all read the same, because telling them apart tells an anonymous caller which addresses and
usernames are in play. That is the same rule /api/auth/otp/verify follows next door.
POST rather than GET, even though the token arrives in an emailed link. A GET is fetched by mail
scanners, link previewers and corporate proxies before the person clicks, and this token is
single use, so a GET route hands them an account creation the recipient never asked for and a
dead link when they do click. The link points at a frontend page that posts here.
It does not sign the caller in. Nothing here proves possession of the device, only of the
mailbox, and there is already an endpoint for turning mailbox possession into a session
(/api/auth/otp/verify) that costs a second round trip and does the MFA and device checks
properly. Minting tokens here would be a fourth issuer path to keep in step with those.
post.summary: POST /api/auth/register/verify. Turns a pending registration into an account, once.

POST /api/client-errors — ingest a small batch of browser errors. Anonymous, because faults
happen before sign-in too; the batch size is limited and strings are capped (see
ClientErrorRecorder) so it can't be used to flood storage. Repeated faults are
deduplicated by fingerprint rather than stored again.
POST /api/client-errors/{id}/resolve: mark an error done, or reopen it.

post.description:
This is how a mapping is checked while the person who wrote it still has it open, and it is the
same code path the sweep takes, so what it reports is what the sweep will do. It answers 200 with
the outcome even when the run failed: the request succeeded, and the outcome is the answer.
            
It waits up to LockWait for another run that is filling the
same collection, the sweep's or another caller's, then answers 409 with Retry-After. See
CollectionSyncLock.
post.summary: Runs one sync now, without waiting for its interval.

post.description:
Every entry goes through what POST /api/contents and PUT /api/contents/{id} run:
the type's create or update permission, the write-path sensitivity rule, the schema validator
and the lifecycle hooks. A push is a faster way in, never a looser one.
            
Nothing is written until every entry has passed, and then everything is written by one
SaveChangesAsync, archiving included. Workflows and their webhooks fire from the committed
events, as for any other write, so each created or changed entry fires once and an unchanged one,
which appends nothing, fires nothing.

parameters.description: The content type, from the route.
parameters.name: type

post.summary:
POST /api/collections/{type}/push: the source that owns a collection's entries writes
them, keyed by slug, in one transaction.

post.description:
Answers with the plan it ran. 400 when a section cannot be applied as written, 403 when the
caller may not make a change it asks for, and 409 when stored state stops a change the way its
own route would refuse it (a field change running on a type it changes, or a field it leaves
out that a block binding names), or when it holds a destructive change and
allowDestructive was not sent. In each of those nothing is written.
post.summary: POST /api/config/apply: converges the caller's tenant to a document, all of it or none of it.

get.description:
Gated, because configuration says a great deal about a deployment: where its connectors point
and who may do what. Each section is also gated on its own read capability, and a section the
caller may not read is named under withheld rather than exported.

parameters.description: The sections to export, comma separated. Left out, every section exported by default is.
parameters.name: sections

get.summary:
GET /api/config/export: the caller's tenant's configuration as one document, in the shape
POST /api/config/apply takes back.

post.summary:
POST /api/config/plan: what applying a document to the caller's tenant would change, refuse or
need. Writes nothing.

get.description:
The rows are WebhookDelivery documents with a connector on them, so the webhook
delivery list's two gates apply unchanged: ViewWorkflowRuns reads
a row, because a delivery is a run's action seen from the wire, and
ViewWebhookResponseBodies reads the response body on it. Not the
connector capabilities: nothing here is a connector's configuration, and the person asking "did
it fire" is the one reading runs.
            
The request headers answer to the narrower capability too, which a webhook row's do not need.
A webhook's headers are all written by this application. A request's are written by an
operator, and reading them where they are configured needs manage_requests.

parameters.description: A connector's slug.
parameters.name: connector

parameters.description: A request definition's slug.
parameters.name: requestSlug

parameters.description: A status class: 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx, or failed for no response at all.
parameters.name: status

get.summary: What Request actions sent through connectors, newest first.
GET /api/content-types/blueprints. The blueprints this instance can apply.

post.description:
Additive, and all or nothing. A type that already exists is a refusal for the whole blueprint
rather than a skip, because a partial apply leaves references pointing at a type whose fields
are not the ones the blueprint assumed, and nothing afterwards says which half arrived.
            
The types are created the way POST /api/content-types creates one: normalized name,
document sourced, sourcing policy recorded against the name. It does not go through the
Portability import, which upserts by name and would overwrite the clash this refuses.
post.summary:
POST /api/content-types/blueprints/{name}. Creates every type the blueprint declares, in the
caller's tenant.

get.description:
A change stopped part way shows the step it is on, how many entries it has rewritten and the
error that stopped it. Another tenant's change, like one that does not exist, is a 404.
get.summary: GET /api/content-types/field-changes/{id}: where a field change is.

post.description:
For a change whose job stopped, for example after the queue gave up on it. The job starts from
the step and entry the change last recorded, so nothing done is done twice. A completed change
is a 409: there is nothing left to run. So is a change whose job is still queued or running, which
would otherwise run beside the new one.
post.summary: POST /api/content-types/field-changes/{id}/resume: queues a running change's job again.

post.description:
The missing half of "content types are defined at runtime".
            
A type could be created and its fields read, but nothing could add one afterwards. The only way
to gain a field was the SEO endpoint, which does exactly this mutation for one hardcoded set, so
the capability was already here and only the general case was missing. Without it a client
asking for one more field on a type that already holds their content had no answer that did not
involve recreating the type, and a page type could never gain the field a block or widget list
needs.
            
Four things this deliberately refuses.
            
A name the type already has, rather than overwriting it. The existing field may have been
renamed, made required or given rules by someone else, and none of that is this endpoint's to
undo. Changing a field is a different operation with data consequences and does not exist yet.
            
A required field with no default, on a type that already has entries. Every one of those entries
is missing the new field, so the type would be declaring an invariant its own content breaks. A
default makes the rule honest, and an optional field is always safe.
            
Anything the create validator would refuse. The merged field list goes through
IContentTypeValidatorService, the same call create makes, so a bad type name, a reference with no
target, or a duplicate under a different casing is rejected here for the same reason and with the
same message.
            
A field that is not Public, on an event-sourced type. The rule create and
SetFieldSensitivity apply: a stream is append-only, so a value written to it cannot be
erased, and a type that could not be created with such a field must not gain one here.
            
The endpoint itself and the optional field it added to a response were additive. The refusals
are request validation, and tightening one is a change to the API contract.

parameters.description: The content type to add to, from the route.
parameters.name: name

post.summary: POST /api/content-types/{name}/fields. Adds one field to a content type that already exists.

post.description:
A label is additive: it touches no entry and is applied at once (200). A rename, a convert (a
new type, with a mapping for the stored values) and a remove touch every entry, so each is a
FieldChange applied by a job (202), whose progress
GET /api/content-types/field-changes/{id} reports and which
POST /api/content-types/field-changes/{id}/resume runs again after it stopped.
            
While a change runs, the field is read under its old name: the job copies every value to the
new name first, then renames the field, then drops the old key. Entry writes to the type are
refused until it completes, so no write lands between two batches in a shape the job has
already passed. One change at a time per type.
            
A rename carries every block binding that sorts or filters on the field along, in the step that
renames the field on the type. A remove is refused with 409 while a binding names the field.
            
A change that drops stored values is destructive: a remove always, and a convert when some value
neither maps to nor reads as a value of the new type. It is refused unless the request says
allowDestructive, and the refusal names how many entries hold a value it would drop.
post.summary:
POST /api/content-types/{name}/fields/{field}/change: changes one field of a type that may
already hold entries, and says what kind of change it was.

put.description:
Its own endpoint for the reason SetFieldOptions is: there is no general field update. It
is how a money field stored before currencies existed gets one, with no pass over its entries.
            
No entry is rewritten. An amount that already fits the scale is untouched and is now read in the
declared currency. Entries holding an amount with more decimal places than the scale, or a value
that is not a number, are counted, and the change is refused unless force is set: each of
them is refused on its next save until the amount is corrected. Changing from one code to
another on a field that entries hold amounts in is refused the same way, because nothing is
converted and every stored amount would be read under the new code.
            
Only the currency and scale are validated, not the whole type and not the field's name, so a
type created before some later rule existed can still declare one.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/fields/{field}/currency, which declares, changes or clears the
currency of one money field.

put.description:
Its own endpoint for the reason SetFieldSensitivity is: there is no general field update,
because a field's name, type and target are load bearing once entries exist. Options are the one
part of a choice that has to keep changing after it is in use. A size sells out, a label is
reworded, a new area of focus is added.
            
Rewording a label or adding an option changes no entry, because entries store the value. Removing
an option that entries still hold is refused unless force is set, with the count of entries
affected. Those entries are left as they are, since rewriting them would mean choosing a
replacement on the client's behalf.
            
Only this field is validated, not the whole type, so a type created before some later rule
existed can still have its options changed.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/fields/{field}/options, which replaces the options of one choice
field.

put.description:
Its own endpoint for the reason SetFieldOptions is: there is no general field update. It
is how a field stored before these members existed gets them, and no entry is read or written,
because none of the three changes what an entry may hold.
            
Only the three members are validated, not the whole type and not the field's name, so a type
created before some later rule existed can still take a hint.
            
A role another field of the type holds is refused, not moved. Which field is the title decides
what a feed reader shows, so taking it from one field is a call of its own.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/fields/{field}/presentation, which sets or clears the editor
hint, the section and the role of one field.

put.description:
Its own endpoint rather than a general content-type update, for the reason
SetPublicDelivery is: this decides who may read data that already exists, which is worth
making on purpose and worth being able to audit, rather than something that rides along inside a
larger edit. A general update is a separate decision, because field names, field types and a
reference target are load-bearing once entries exist.
            
The two directions are not symmetric, and treating them as one operation is the mistake this is
shaped to avoid.
            
RAISING (Public towards Hidden) is safe for the future and does nothing about the past. The value
stops being served, which is what the caller wants. It is still in the entry's data, in every
backup and in the event stream, and nothing here removes it from any of those.
            
Raising is also not finished when the definition is updated. Anonymous search matches against
Content.SearchText, a derived column built from the fields that were Public when the entry
was last written. Flipping the definition changes what is returned and not what is matched, so a
caller could still search for a value they may no longer read and learn which entries contain it,
one guess at a time. The search text is rebuilt for that reason, and it is rebuilt BEFORE the
definition changes so no window exists where the old text is still matchable under the new
level. Both happen as one FieldChange: applied before the answer for a type that
fits in one batch, and by the job queue for a larger one, with the change in the response.
            
LOWERING is a disclosure. Every value written while the field was masked becomes readable to
everyone who can read the type, retroactively, and to anonymous callers as well when the type is
publicly deliverable. It is allowed, because refusing it would make raising a one-way door and a
field marked Sensitive by mistake would need direct database access to recover, which is the
failure SetPublicDelivery exists to answer. It is allowed only with
acknowledgeDisclosure, and it is recorded under its own audit action so it can be alerted
on. Lowering updates the definition FIRST and rebuilds the search text after, which is the same
rule the other way round: whichever step exposes less goes first.
            
It deliberately does not run IContentTypeValidatorService. That validates a whole type on
create and has no rules about sensitivity, so all it could do here is refuse the request for
something unrelated: a type created before the "a reference must name its target" rule existed
would fail it, and masking a leaking field on that type would become impossible.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/fields/{field}/sensitivity, which changes one field's sensitivity
and brings the entries already written under the old level into line with it.

put.description:
The same gate as turning public delivery on, because it is the same decision: what an anonymous
caller can read. A field that is Sensitive, Hidden or a token cannot be in the returned set, and
a reveal may add a token but no other non-Public field.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/lookup, which sets or removes the anonymous lookup the type answers
at POST /api/public/{type}/lookup.

put.description:
The rule says which field takes the number and which strategy hands it out, so the cost of the
choice is visible where it is made (see NumberStrategy). Changing the strategy keeps
the series' count. Entries that already exist keep what they hold; only entries created from now
on are numbered.
put.summary: PUT /api/content-types/{name}/numbering: sets or clears the rule that numbers a type's new entries.

put.description:
This exists because the opt-in would otherwise be a one-way door. Public delivery became opt-in so
that modelling members or a ledger as content no longer hands out an anonymous endpoint nobody
asked for — but content types have no update endpoint, so on upgrade every existing type stops
being delivered with no supported way to turn it back on. A site serving a blog this way would
have needed direct database access to recover.
            
Deliberately its own endpoint rather than a general content-type update: enabling anonymous access
to a whole content type is a decision worth making on purpose, and worth being able to audit,
rather than something that rides along inside a larger edit.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/public-delivery — turn anonymous public delivery on or off for one
content type.

parameters.description: The content type to rebuild, from the route.
parameters.name: name

put.description:
Its own endpoint because content types have no general update, and a type stored before the
template existed has no other way to get one. No entry is read or written: the template is
applied when a feed or a sitemap is built.
            
Both of those answer with a one minute cache lifetime, so a change shows in them after that.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/route-template, which sets or clears the path the feed and the
sitemap build an entry's link from.

post.description:
An endpoint rather than a checkbox on the type, because opting in is adding fields and this is
the one place that has to be true: the fields must arrive through the same shape everything else
reads, or delivery, validation and the admin form each need a special case for SEO.
            
Additive and idempotent. A field the type already has is reported and left alone rather than
overwritten, because a client may well have renamed the display name, made one required, or
changed a type, and none of that is this endpoint's to undo.
post.summary: POST /api/content-types/{name}/seo-fields. Adds the SEO field set to a content type.

put.description:
Its own endpoint for the reason the route template has one: content types have no general
update. No entry is read or written. The block is built when an entry is read by slug, and the
type's updatedAt moves, so a cached read revalidates.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/structured-data, which sets or clears the schema.org type a
single delivered entry of the type is described as.

put.description:
Its own endpoint because content types have no general update, and a type stored before rules
existed has no other way to get one.
            
No entry is read into memory or rewritten. For each rule added or changed, the entries that
already share their values with another entry the rule counts are counted in the database, and
the change is refused with 409 unless force is set. With it the rule is stored and those
entries stay as they are: each can still be edited, moved and erased, and only a write that
would bring an entry to values another entry holds is refused. The count is a reading taken
before the save, and a write that read the type before the save lands can still add to it.
put.summary:
PUT /api/content-types/{name}/uniqueness, which sets the type's uniqueness rules: the values only
one entry may hold at a time.

get.description:
How an operator finds the entries a rule declared with force left as they were. Read in
the database, a page at a time; the values are compared there exactly as a write compares them.
            
Ids only, and only of entries the caller may read: the capability that declares rules, read on
the type, and the type's row rules applied to each entry as the entries list applies them, since
the list says which entries exist.
get.summary:
GET /api/content-types/{name}/uniqueness/{rule}/duplicates, the entries that share their values
under a rule with another entry the rule counts, oldest first.

parameters.description: Matches any string value in an entry's data, case-insensitively.
parameters.name: search

parameters.description: One status, or null for every status.
parameters.name: status

get.description:
For a signed-in viewer on a public site. GET /api/public/{type}/{slug} is anonymous and
serves only published, publicly deliverable entries, so a page gated by a role had no way to be
fetched by the slug in its URL. This applies the permission check GET /api/contents/{id}
applies, to any status, and returns the same response built by EntryResponse, masking
included.
            
An entry the caller may not read answers 404, not the 403 the id route gives. A slug is readable
text a caller can guess, and any signed-in account, a self-registered one with no content
permission included, reaches this route, so a 403 would confirm that a draft or another user's
entry exists under that slug. An id is not guessable, which is why the id route can say 403.
            
Not gated on IsPubliclyDeliverable. That flag decides what anonymous callers get; here the
read permission decides.

parameters.description: The content type name, as in GET /api/public/{type}/{slug}.
parameters.name: type

parameters.description: Matched case-insensitively against the type's slug field, the same way delivery matches it.
parameters.name: slug

get.summary: The authoring read of one entry, addressed by type and slug instead of id.

get.description:
Each type is counted under the read predicate ReadPredicateAsync
compiles for the caller, the one the list endpoint pages with, so the numbers agree with what
GET /api/contents would list. A type whose rules do not compile is named in
UncountedTypes rather than loaded row by row: the cost of the answer stays a handful of
counts however large the collection is.
Types the caller reads unconditionally are counted together, so a caller who reads everything
costs four queries whatever the number of types. Across types, the types are the stored content
type definitions, so an entry whose type has no definition is not counted.

parameters.description: One content type, or null for every type the caller may read.
parameters.name: contentType

get.summary:
GET /api/contents/counts, how many entries the caller may read, by status, so an overview card
can say "121 published, 27 draft" without paging the whole collection.

delete.description:
Separate from a status change to Archived, and deliberately not the same verb. Archiving is
reversible and keeps the history; this is neither, and an endpoint whose name does not say so
invites someone to reach for it when they meant to unpublish.
            
SuperAdmin only. This is the one operation in the product that destroys the audit trail's own
subject matter, so it sits at the highest role rather than with content editing.
delete.summary:
DELETE /api/contents/{id}/erase. Removes a content item and its history irrecoverably, for a
right-to-erasure request.

put.summary:
PUT /api/contents/{Id}/schedule. Arms (or clears) the times at which the scheduler will publish a
Draft or unpublish (Archive) a Published item. The times are stored on the content read model as
intent; ScheduledContentService consumes them on its sweep and
emits a real ContentStatusChanged event for each transition. Requires the same "update" permission as
a status change.

get.description:
Tokens POST /api/preview issued are left out, here and in revoke. A caller with read
alone can mint them, each is gone in 30 minutes, and listed they would push the links an editor
made down the page.
get.summary: GET /api/contents/{id}/share-links: this entry's links, newest first, without keys or hashes.

post.description:
With path it is a page link, without it an entry link. Both open the same thing, this
entry; the path is only carried to whoever opens the link.
post.summary: POST /api/contents/{id}/share-links: create a link to this one entry and return its key once.

delete.summary:
DELETE /api/contents/{id}/share-links/{linkId}: revoke one of this entry's links. Revoking twice
is still 204. A link that belongs to another entry, or to the whole site, is 404 here, and so is
a preview token, which the list does not show either.

get.summary: GET /api/devices — the signed-in user's own devices, current one flagged.

post.summary: POST /api/devices/{id}/revoke — revoke one of the signed-in user's own devices.

post.description:
For whoever writes workflows, so it asks for manage_workflows. On top of that the caller
must be able to read the template and the entry, checked as GET /api/contents/{id} checks
them, and the entry is rendered as that read shows it: a Sensitive field the caller may not see
is empty here, and a reference is followed only to entries the caller may read. A run resolves
against the whole entry, so the preview can show less than the email; it never shows more.
            
A template the caller cannot read answers 404, like one that does not exist, since a slug can be
guessed. An entry the caller cannot read answers 403, as the read by id does.

parameters.description: The template's id or slug, from the route.
parameters.name: id

post.summary:
POST /api/email-templates/{id}/preview. Renders a template's subject and body against an entry,
as a workflow would send them, and sends nothing.

get.summary:
GET /api/feature-flags — every flag's on/off result for the current request (tenant + user), so
the frontend can gate UI. Anonymous-friendly: public pages get flags evaluated with just the club,
and see only the flags marked public. An unauthenticated caller is not told the key of anything
else, since the name alone reads as a roadmap.
GET /api/feature-flags/admin — all flags with their full config.

post.summary: POST /api/feature-flags/admin — create or update a flag (upsert by key).
POST /api/feature-flags/admin/{key}/toggle — flip a flag on/off.

parameters.description: A case-insensitive substring of the file name, for a picker's search box.
parameters.name: q

parameters.description: A content type, or a prefix of one such as image/.
parameters.name: contentType

get.summary:
GET /api/files. The uploads in this tenant, newest first, without the cached resizes: a variant
is reached as ?w= on its original and has no row of its own here, as on the downloads.

post.summary:
POST /api/files. Uploads a single file (image or PDF). Bytes go through the configured
IFileStorage (Postgres or S3); metadata is recorded in Postgres. Pass a form field
isPublic=true to make it anonymously readable; the default is private (fail closed).

parameters.description: Delete even though entries still reference the file.
parameters.name: force

delete.summary:
DELETE /api/files/{id}. Removes the record, its cached resizes and the bytes behind all of them.
Refused with a 409 while an entry still references the file, unless ?force=true, so an
editor cannot break a page without being told which one. Refused with a 403 if the caller is not
the uploader and does not hold manage_all_files, the same rule Download applies; see
FileAccessRule.

parameters.description: Requested width in pixels, as ?w=400. Absent means the file unchanged.
parameters.name: w

get.summary:
GET /api/files/{id} — authenticated download of any file. If the file lives on an object store with
a public URL, redirects there; otherwise streams the bytes from the configured storage.
Add ?w=400 for a narrower copy of an image; see docs/image-variants.md.

patch.summary:
PATCH /api/files/{id}. Sets the alt text and caption. Nothing else about a file is editable:
the name, type and public flag are decided at upload and a frontend may have cached the answer.

get.summary: GET /api/files/{id}/meta. The record without the bytes, for an editor's file panel.

GET /api/files/{id}/usage. The entries in this tenant whose data references the file, newest
change first. See FileUsage for what counts as a reference and what a row shows.
GET /api/forms. The content types that accept public submissions, paged.

put.description:
Refuses a type with a required field a visitor cannot fill in, because every submission to it
would fail validation and the form would look broken rather than misconfigured. Refuses a
singleton type, which could only ever take one submission. Refuses to verify a field that is not
an email field a visitor can fill in, since no submission could ever pass.
            
Turning a form off deletes its row, as it always has, and keeps the field it verified beside
its send count. Turning it on again without verifyEmailField puts that field back, so a
client that has never heard of the setting cannot drop verification by toggling the form.
put.summary: PUT /api/forms/{contentType}. Turns public submissions on or off for one content type.

post.summary:
POST /api/import/analyze, which accepts an .xlsx/CSV upload and return a typed preview grid so a UI can
build a column mapping. Parses only; nothing is stored. Any authenticated user may analyze.

post.description:
The constructor keeps the services it took before this endpoint moved onto
IContentCreator, because it is public in a published package. The creator is
resolved per request instead.
post.summary:
POST /api/import/content — bulk-create content items from mapped records (typically the output of
/api/import/analyze after column mapping). Reuses the CMS's content-type validation, per-type
create permission, and event-sourced creation; all creates commit in one transaction.

post.description:
Authorised like the bulk create: the target content type's own create permission, checked for
the type and again for each row as stored. One request, one transaction. Bounded by the upload
size, the expanded size, MaxRecords data rows and
MaxSeconds; past any of them the answer is a refusal and nothing is
written. A crash or timeout midway rolls the transaction back, so there is no half import. A
second run creates the entries again, so use dryRun first; a uniqueness rule on the type
refuses the repeats.
post.summary:
POST /api/import/spreadsheet. Uploads an .xlsx/CSV with the header row, content type and column
mapping, and creates an entry from every data row, not only the 500 analyze previews.

parameters.description: Only this source, for example client-errors. Null reads every source the caller may read.
parameters.name: source

parameters.description: Filter by resolved state. Null means both.
parameters.name: resolved

parameters.description: How far back to look, in days. 30 when unset.
parameters.name: days

get.summary:
GET /api/incidents: one paged list across client errors, dead-lettered jobs, failed workflow
actions and failed deliveries, grouped by fingerprint and redacted here, so no client has to
regroup or re-redact and nothing personal leaves the API on the way (#893).

get.description:
The session is the request's tenant-scoped one, so the filter that keeps one tenant's jobs from
another is Marten's, the same as every other list here. Nothing in this endpoint reaches across.

parameters.description: One of JobState. Null = every state.
parameters.name: state

get.summary: GET /api/jobs, newest first, for the tenant of the request.

get.description:
No request: nothing in the query or the route can name another user. The answer is always the
UserId the token carries.
The tenant is the token's own tenant claim when it has one, else the resolved tenant.
Routes under /api/me are exempt from the check that a token's tenant matches the
resolved one, so an X-Tenant header here could otherwise ask about a tenant the session
does not act in. Every other route refuses that session there anyway.
An API key gets a 403 from ApiKeyScopeProcessor, as
on every route outside the content API. The response is sent Cache-Control: no-store
through the /api/me entry in
IsNoStorePath.
get.summary:
GET /api/me, the signed-in caller's own roles and capabilities in the current tenant, read from
the store the way the API decides access, so a console can decide sensitivity and navigation the
same way. The seeded SuperAdmin role is SuperAdminRoleId in the list.

post.summary:
POST /api/me/password — the signed-in user changes their own password. It re-verifies the current
password first (so an idle-but-stolen session can't silently take over the account), enforces the
password policy, stores a fresh BCrypt hash, and revokes the user's refresh tokens. Existing
short-lived access tokens are not individually killed; they expire on their own. It lives under the
global /api/me identity prefix, so it is not tenant-scoped — a user is global.

get.summary: GET /api/me/profile — the signed-in user's social profile (name, photo, birthday, location).

put.summary:
PUT /api/me/profile, the signed-in user sets their own display name. It sits under the global
/api/me identity prefix like the password change, so it is not tenant-scoped.

post.description:
It exchanges, it does not renew. The new token expires when the presented one would have, and the
presented one is revoked, so a chain of switches cannot keep a bearer alive past its original
expiry. It returns no refresh token: the one the caller already holds is not tied to a tenant, since
a refresh mints for the X-Tenant it is sent and re-checks membership.
post.summary:
POST /api/me/switch: the signed-in user exchanges their access token for one scoped to another
tenant, without re-authenticating. The issuer checks for an active membership in the target tenant
(or treats it as unmanaged, as every token path does) and bakes that tenant's roles into the new
token. Device binding (the did claim) is carried over so device-trust still holds.

get.description:
LogoUrl is the Logo of each tenant's published site entry, which costs two reads
for every tenant on the page and none for the rest, so at most two hundred for a full page.
The roles cost one more read for the whole page, since the memberships are already loaded.
get.summary:
GET /api/me/tenants — the tenants the signed-in user belongs to (their active memberships joined
with the tenant registry). Powers a "switch tenant" experience across a multi-tenant deployment.

get.description:
Signed-in callers only, like GET /api/meta beside it, and not role-restricted: anyone
editing a content type needs the field types. The three other parts repeat what
GET /api/capabilities, GET /api/workflows/actions and GET /api/modules
already return, so each is left out for a caller those endpoints would refuse.
            
Every list is read from memory. The database is read only to answer the three capability
checks: each is a user load, a membership lookup and a role query the first time, and is then
answered by the permission cache, which keys on the capability. So a cold request is three
checks of up to three queries each, and a warm one is none.
            
The response is not kept by a cache, whatever its status: the route is one of
IsNoStorePath's.
get.summary:
GET /api/meta/describe, what this instance accepts: field types and the rules each takes, the
editor hints and roles a field may declare, and for a caller who may read them the
capabilities, workflow actions and running modules.

get.description:
Read from the ModuleCatalogue AddBarakoCMS built, which holds what the host
added or discovery found, not a list somebody maintains alongside it. The catalogue rather than
the IBarakoModule singletons, because those hold only the modules the enabled list
let run, and a module switched off by configuration is still installed.
            
Gated on Roles("SuperAdmin", "Admin") rather than on a capability. Every name in
SystemCapabilities covers a management surface this endpoint neither reads nor
writes. See issue #185 for the whole argument, and
RoleGateTests.The_core_routes_still_on_a_role_name_are_the_two_that_are_meant_to_be for the
pinned list this belongs to now that #443 has migrated everything else.
get.summary:
GET /api/modules, reporting every module this instance saw, whether it runs, and what the
schema preflight found for it.

get.description:
A caller who holds view_module_configuration only through a tenant role sees the keys a
module marks as tenant scope. Deployment scope keys are left out, not redacted, the same split
as the settings routes (PlatformScope).
            
An unknown module and a disabled one both answer 404 with no body, and the name asked for is
never echoed.
get.summary:
GET /api/modules/{name}/configuration, the configuration an enabled module runs with and where
each value came from. Read only. No secret leaves through it: see
ModuleConfigurationReader for the order of the checks.
Numbers in a range of an external series that were never recorded.
GET /api/pages/settings: the tenant's page tree settings, and what they come to.

put.description:
A replace, not a merge: a value left out goes back to the deployment's. Sending every value null
leaves the tenant reading Modules:Pages alone, as a tenant that never set any does.
put.summary: PUT /api/pages/settings: replaces the tenant's page tree settings.

get.description:
Each entry passes the same read check GET /api/contents/{id} applies, and its data is masked
the same way before a title or slug is read from it. A page whose parent the caller cannot see, or
whose chain loops, is listed at the top level so it can still be found and fixed. path is
null for a page whose chain does not reach a root. At most MaxPages
pages are read, oldest first, and truncated says when there were more.
get.summary:
GET /api/pages/tree: every page the caller may read, drafts included, nested and ordered, for the
console.

put.description:
Refuses a type with no lifecycle, or whose lifecycle lacks the named transitions, because a
payment could never move the entry. Refuses an amount field that is not a number field.
put.summary: PUT /api/payments/payable/{contentType}. Declares what is payable on a content type, or stops it.

post.description:
An event is handled once. Its provider event id is the key of a stored record, saved in the same
commit as the transition, so a redelivery finds the record and answers 200 without doing
anything, and two deliveries racing each other cannot both commit. A bad signature answers 401
and touches nothing. The transition runs as the system actor payments-webhook, on the
module's own authority, since no user is behind a webhook.
            
An event for a payment whose entry is no longer in the state the transition starts from answers
409 and writes nothing, so the attempt stays pending for a person or for reconciliation.
post.summary:
POST /api/payments/webhooks/{provider}. Anonymous, because the provider holds no token; the
signature the provider's adapter checks is the authentication.

get.summary: GET /api/portability/export?types=member,event — download a content bundle (all types if omitted).

post.description:
Every type goes through the checks POST /api/content-types and add field run, and every
record through the same write path as POST /api/contents: write-side sensitivity keyed on
the caller, schema validation, lifecycle hooks and the type's initial state.
            
All or nothing. Any refused type or record answers 400 naming each one, as
contentTypes[i] or contents[i], and nothing is written. Partial success was the
other choice and it is the worse one here: import always creates new entries, so rerunning a
half-applied bundle after fixing it would duplicate everything that landed the first time. A dry
run refuses exactly what the real run would.
post.summary:
POST /api/portability/import. Upserts content types (by name) then recreates content via events.
Pass dryRun: true to preview the counts without writing.

post.description:
The token is the key of an entry share link stored with Preview set:
hashed, looked up in the caller's tenant, expired by the server and deleted with its entry. The
caller needs read on the entry, the same check as the authoring read, so a token cannot be had
for a draft the caller may not see. The body and the status codes are what they were when the
token was a signed JWT.
            
Read is a low bar and the route used to store nothing, so a token leaves as little behind as it
can: a fixed label, no audit row, no place in the entry's list of links, and at most
MaxPreviewPerEntry live per entry, the oldest dropped to make room.
            
The Deprecation header is set here, so it is on what this handler answers: the 200, its
404s and the 401 for a token whose user is gone. It is not on an answer written before the
handler runs: the 401 for no credentials, a 400 from binding, a 429, or the 403 an API key gets.
post.summary:
POST /api/preview: a signed-in editor gets a 30 minute token for one draft entry. Deprecated in
favour of an entry share link (POST /api/contents/{id}/share-links).

get.description: 404 for a bad, expired, spent or revoked link, and for a user who may no longer make the move.
get.summary:
GET /api/public/action-links/{token}: what confirming the link would do. Changes nothing, so a
mail scanner that follows the link approves nothing.

post.description:
The permission and row conditions are checked by the transitioner at this moment, not read from
the link. The mark that spends the link is stored in the same commit as the transition, so a
refused move leaves the link usable and a second use finds it spent. A bad, expired, spent or
revoked link, and a user who may no longer make the move, all answer 404.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/action-links/{token}: makes the transition the link is for, as the user it is
for, and spends the link.

get.description:
The range is at most MaxRangeDays days. An unknown or inactive
resource answers 404, the same for both. Throttled per client IP.

parameters.description: The id of the resource.
parameters.name: resource

parameters.description: Start of the range, ISO 8601 with a UTC offset. A + in the offset must be sent as %2B.
parameters.name: from

parameters.description: End of the range, exclusive, in the same form.
parameters.name: to

get.summary:
GET /api/public/availability?resource=&from=&to=. Anonymous. The free slots of a resource in
a range, and nothing about the bookings that took the rest.

get.description:
Off unless Delivery:Events:Enabled is true, and 404 while it is off, the same answer
an OAuth provider gives when it is not configured. The literal events segment wins over
/api/public/{type}, so a content type named "events" is not reachable by that route.
            
?type= repeats to filter by content type. A type that is not deliverable simply never
matches, which says nothing about whether it exists.
get.summary:
GET /api/public/events: a server-sent event stream of the tenant's content changes.
Anonymous like the rest of public delivery, and answering to the same rules: only entries of a
publicly deliverable type, only while Published, only the fields the type marks Public.

parameters.description: Requested width in pixels, as ?w=400. Absent means the file unchanged.
parameters.name: w

get.summary:
GET /api/public/files/{id} — anonymous read of a PUBLIC file for a website frontend. Anything not
marked public returns 404 (fail closed; indistinguishable from missing, so private ids can't be
probed). For an object store it redirects to the object's public URL; for Postgres it proxies the
bytes. The literal "files" segment wins over the /api/public/{type}/{slug} content route.
Add ?w=400 for a narrower copy of an image; see docs/image-variants.md.

parameters.description:
A width in pixels, as ?w=640 on the download. The size, width and height answered are
then those of the copy that download serves, which is a narrower variant or the original. A
width the download refuses is ignored.
parameters.name: w

get.summary: GET /api/public/files/{id}/meta. Anonymous, for a PUBLIC file only, so an can carry the alt text an editor wrote. Anything not public is a 404, indistinguishable from missing, exactly as the bytes next door: metadata is not less private than the file it describes. With ?w= it describes the copy the download would serve at that width, so a frontend can write a srcset with each variant's own width and height.

GET /api/public/forms/{slug}. Anonymous. The fields a widget draws, which are exactly the fields
the submit endpoint accepts: nothing non-Public, nothing of a type a form cannot render.

post.description:
The request has no status, sensitivity or owner, so a caller cannot choose them: status is always
Draft, sensitivity always Sensitive and the owner always empty. Unknown fields are refused rather
than dropped, with the same message as a field that exists but is not submittable, so the refusal
does not tell a stranger which hidden fields a type has.
            
A form that verifies an email field also needs emailVerificationCode, the code its
email-code route sent to the address in that field. A form that does not verify never
reads it.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/forms/{slug}. Anonymous. Stores the submission as a Draft entry of the form's
content type with document sensitivity Sensitive, so public delivery never serves it back.

post.description:
Answers 202 with the same body whether the mail went out, the provider refused it or the
honeypot was filled. A limit is never silent: the per client limit, the per address limit and
the per form limit each answer 429. A form that does not verify answers 404, so this route sends
nothing on a form whose owner did not turn verification on.
            
Nothing from the request reaches the message. The recipient is the address after the email field
check, which admits no whitespace, and the subject and body are built from the form's own name.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/forms/{slug}/email-code. Anonymous. Emails a one-time code to the address, for
a form that verifies an email field.

get.description:
A flagged page whose parent is not flagged sits under its nearest flagged ancestor, or at the top
when it has none, and keeps its real path. A page with no path (under a draft, a Sensitive page or
a missing parent) is left out, since its URL would not resolve.
            
At most MaxPages published pages are read, oldest first, and
truncated says when there were more. A page past the limit, and every page under it, is
missing from the menu while resolve still serves it, so a renderer needs to be told.
get.summary:
GET /api/public/pages/navigation: the nested, ordered tree of published pages flagged for
navigation, each with its absolute path.

get.description:
The core slug route cannot tell /about/team from /careers/team. This looks up the pages holding the
last segment's slug, walks each one's parents, and answers with the one whose whole path matches.
Every page on the walk has to be published and Public, so a published page under a draft does not
resolve. The walk reads at most MaxDepth ancestors per candidate.
get.summary:
GET /api/public/pages/resolve?path=/about/team: the published page at a path, with its canonical
path and breadcrumbs from the root down to itself. 404 when nothing is served there.

post.description:
The request names an entry and a provider and nothing else. The amount, the currency and the
description come from the entry and its type's payable declaration, so a body that carries an
amount is read as if it did not. An entry whose type is not payable, or that is not in the state
the paid transition starts from, or that has already been paid, answers the same way it would
if it did not exist or could not be paid, so the route does not describe other entries.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/payments/checkout. Anonymous. Starts a payment for one entry and returns the
provider's hosted checkout URL.

get.description:
This runs on the 404 path, which is when a site is already having a bad time, so it is one
indexed equality lookup and nothing else. No wildcards, no regular expressions, no scan.
            
Anonymous because the caller is a frontend rendering a page for a visitor who has no session. A
redirect map is not a secret: every entry in it is a URL that used to be public and a URL that is
public now. It is still per tenant, because the document is conjoined and the session carries the
tenant, so one site cannot read another's.
            
The 404 is deliberately the same shape as any other miss. A frontend asks this exactly once, when
its own lookup failed, and an empty 200 would make "no redirect" and "a redirect to nowhere" the
same answer.
get.summary: GET /api/public/redirects/resolve?path=/old. Anonymous, and answers 404 when nothing moved.

post.description:
The key travels in the body, so it is in no URL, no access log and no Referer. 200 or 404 and
nothing else: a wrong key, an expired or revoked link, another tenant's key, a preview token
and a link whose entry is gone or can no longer be delivered all answer the same 404. The
request names no entry, so there is no id for a caller to change.
            
A preview token is refused so that it has one use, the ?preview= query it was issued for.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/site/share-links/open: what this key opens for the resolved tenant, and for an
entry or page link the entry itself.

post.description:
200 or 404 and nothing else. A wrong key, an expired or revoked link, another tenant's key and a
key that opens one entry all answer the same 404, so the route says nothing about which links
exist. An entry or page key has to be refused here: a frontend reads this 200 as leave to show
the whole held site.
post.summary: POST /api/public/site/share-links/redeem: is this key a live link to the whole site for the resolved tenant.

get.description:
A field is listed exactly when ToPublic would deliver its value,
by the same IsDeliveredField. Those names are already in every
delivered entry, so this widens nothing. A Sensitive or Hidden field is not named, and neither its sensitivity, its rules, its
default nor its visible roles are returned for any field.
A type that is not publicly deliverable answers 404, the same as an unknown one, so the route
cannot confirm which types exist.
Three segments under /api/public/ on purpose. A content type name may be any text, so a
literal in the first or second segment would be a type name too: /api/public/types/{type}
takes /api/public/types/{slug} from a type named types. Every route a content type
is read on, {type}, {type}/search, {type}/semantic, {type}/feed.xml
and {type}/{slug}, is at most two, so this route shadows none of them.
get.summary:
GET /api/public/types/{type}/description, what a renderer needs to build titles, links, a
sitemap and a feed from a publicly deliverable type's own declaration: its route template, and
the name, type, role and editor hint of each Public field.

parameters.description: Only entries updated after this instant. Optional.
parameters.name: changedSince

get.summary: GET /api/public/{type} — paged Published entries of a content type, masked and cacheable.

GET /api/public/{type}/feed.xml — an RSS 2.0 feed of the newest Published, document-Public entries of
a content type. It reuses the same projection as the rest of public delivery, so drafts, Sensitive
documents, and non-Public fields never appear. The literal "feed.xml" segment wins over the {slug}
route. Anonymous and cacheable.
            
Item links point at the tenant's site: the Url of its published site entry, else
Feeds:SiteUrl (see EntryUrls), and per type
the type's route template or Feeds:Paths:{type} (a template like /blog/{slug};
defaults to /{type}/{slug}). An item's title,
description and date come from the fields the type gives the title, summary and date roles,
and from the field names guessed before roles existed when it gives none or the field is empty.
With no site entry Url and neither Feeds:SiteUrl nor App:BaseUrl set,
the feed answers 503 unless AllowedHosts makes the request host trustworthy, because a feed
is fetched by aggregators and its links must not come from a header the caller wrote (#147).

post.description:
Every way of not finding an entry answers the same empty 404: a type that does not exist or
answers no lookup, a reference nobody holds, and a reference whose identifier does not match. So
the route cannot be used to learn that a reference exists. The match runs in Postgres on the
reference alone and the identifier is compared afterwards, so both misses cost the same query.
A POST, so the identifier, a last name or an email, is in the body and not in a URL a proxy logs.
Throttled twice: per tenant and visitor by LookupPolicy, and per
reference by LookupReferenceThrottle, which is taken before anything is read.
Any entry of the type but an Archived one is found, whatever its status, because the records a
lookup is for (registrations, orders) are rarely Published. The answer carries only fields that
are Public and not tokens at the moment of the read, plus the reveal fields while the setting is
on, and is never cached.
post.summary:
POST /api/public/{type}/lookup: one entry, found by a reference plus an identifier, with only the
fields the type names.

get.summary:
GET /api/public/{type}/search?q=…&limit=… — top public matches for a query. The literal "search"
segment wins over the {slug} route. Matching runs ONLY over allowlisted public fields (the entry is
projected to its public shape first), so a draft, a document-Sensitive entry, or a non-Public field
can never surface a result. A title/name hit outranks a body hit. Scans a bounded, recent window;
swap in Postgres full-text search for larger corpora. Takes the list route's
filter[field][op]=value parameters, applied in the query before the scan cap and the limit.

GET /api/public/{type}/semantic?q=…&limit=… — vector search over a type's index. Embeds the query,
ranks stored vectors by cosine similarity, then re-verifies each candidate is STILL Published and
document-Public before returning it — so an entry unpublished or hidden since indexing never leaks.
Anonymous and cacheable; the literal "semantic" segment wins over the {slug} route. Takes the
delivery list's filter[field][op]=value parameters, applied before ranking.

get.description:
404 for every refusal, so a caller cannot tell a missing entry from a draft, a field the type
does not allow from one that is empty. The entry goes through the same projector the core public
routes use, so it has to be published, Public, of a deliverable type, and the field has to be
marked Public on that type, on top of being listed in Fields.

parameters.description: png or svg. Defaults to png.
parameters.name: format

parameters.description: Pixels per QR module. Defaults to 8.
parameters.name: size

get.summary: GET /api/public/{type}/{id}/qr/{field}?format=png|svg&size=8: one field's value as a QR code.

GET /api/public/{type}/{slug} — a single Published entry by slug; 404 if draft/archived/sensitive/missing.
With a valid ?preview=<token> (see PreviewToken),
an unpublished entry is returned too — the token authorizes only that one entry, and the response is
still projected to Public fields and marked no-store. An invalid token falls back to published-only.

GET /api/pwa/installs — devices that have run the app, newest activity first, with who
            (when signed in) and whether they're running it installed. Admin only.

post.summary:
POST /api/pwa/report — the client reports how it's running (installed app vs browser tab), on
launch and on install. Anonymous by default; when a signed-in user reports, their identity is
recorded so the admin can see who installed the app. Idempotent per device.

delete.summary:
Removes a deleted query for good. Mirrors content's archive versus erase split. It only takes a
query that is already deleted, so a live one cannot be destroyed in one call.

post.description:
The same shape as the request dry run and for the same reason: a query is written against a
schema and its rows are read by a third party, and the gap between those is where a recipient
list is wrong in ways nobody sees until it is sent.
post.summary: Runs a saved query and returns the rows, so an operator can see what a payload would carry.

post.description:
Every line is validated against the rules already stored AND against the lines above it in the
same file. Checking only against the database would let one upload introduce a loop that neither
line creates on its own, which is the loop nobody can find afterwards because no single rule
looks wrong.
            
A bad line is rejected and named; the rest still import. That is the opposite of the content
importer next door, which is all or nothing, and the reason is what the two are for: a content
bundle is one export that should arrive whole, and a redirect list is a spreadsheet somebody
typed, where the useful answer is "these four hundred worked and these three did not".
post.summary: POST /api/redirects/import. A site migration brings hundreds of these at once.

put.description:
The renderer is how a tenant's blocks are known: it registers the blocks of the plugins enabled
for the tenant it is serving, named by the request the same way delivery names one. With no
renderer key configured the route answers 404, and a missing or wrong key answers 401, compared
in fixed time. The key is a deployment secret that already lets the renderer skip the per-IP
limit, so whoever holds it can rewrite any tenant's block schema; it opens nothing else here.
The body is capped at MaxBodyBytes, so what is read before the key is
checked is bounded.
put.summary:
PUT /api/renderer/blocks/schema: replaces the tenant's block schema, as the renderer, which sends
the deployment's renderer key in X-Barako-Renderer-Key.

get.summary: GET /api/reports. The tenant's saved reports, paged.

post.description:
Checks the definition against the content type's schema, so a report that names a field the type
does not have, or sums one that is not a number, is refused when it is saved and not on every
run. Whether a given caller may read those fields is decided at run time, by the caller.
post.summary: POST /api/reports. Saves a report definition for the tenant.

get.description:
The caller needs no capability beyond being signed in, and sees only what their own read rules
show: their row conditions narrow the entries counted, and a field they cannot read cannot be the
group, a measure or a filter (403). A role whose rules cannot be written as a database condition
is refused rather than answered by loading every entry.

parameters.description: First day included, on the date field the report names (the day created by default).
parameters.name: from

parameters.description: Last day included.
parameters.name: to

parameters.description: csv for a CSV download. Anything else, or nothing, is JSON.
parameters.name: format

get.summary: GET /api/reports/{name}?from=&to=&format=. Runs a saved report as the caller.

post.description:
The most useful screen in this feature. A template is written against a schema and read by a
third party, and the gap between those is where an integration is wrong in ways nobody sees until
a customer does. Seeing the finished body before anything is sent closes it.
            
No credential appears here. The connector's secrets are attached by the sender, after this, so
there is nothing for this endpoint to redact: it never had one.
post.summary: Composes everything and returns the exact call, without making it.

get.summary: GET /api/roles: the caller's tenant's roles and the platform roles, or every role for a platform caller.
GET /api/roles/deleted: the roles that were deleted and not yet erased, within the caller's reach.

delete.summary:
DELETE /api/roles/{id}/erase: removes a deleted role for good. It only takes a role that is
already deleted, so a live one cannot be destroyed in one call.

post.summary: POST /api/roles/{id}/restore: brings a deleted role back with the permissions it had.

post.description:
To the caller and nowhere else, deliberately. An endpoint that takes a recipient is a way to send
mail from this deployment's domain to any address somebody names, and the person who needs to see
the test is the one who just typed the credentials in.
            
It refuses when no provider is registered rather than reporting success. The mock provider logs
and returns, so a test button in front of it answers "sent" every time and moves the failure to
the first real invoice, which is the thing this endpoint exists to prevent.
post.summary: Sends one email to the caller's own address, so a configuration screen can say whether it worked.

get.summary: GET /api/settings/storage: where this tenant's files go, and whether it can be changed here.

put.description:
Moves no file. Files already stored stay where they are and keep downloading, because each read
follows the provider its file records. Refused with a 409 naming the keys while configuration
sets storage, since configuration would win anyway and a setting that does nothing should not
look saved.
put.summary: PUT /api/settings/storage: where this tenant's new uploads go, from the next request on.

post.description:
A secret left out is taken from the stored setting, so a screen can test a corrected region
without asking for the secret again. Nothing is saved whatever the outcome, and the secret is in
no answer, including the provider's error message, which never quotes it.
post.summary:
POST /api/settings/storage/test: puts, reads and deletes a small object with the settings sent,
without saving them, and says which step failed.

get.summary: GET /api/site/share-links: the tenant's links, newest first, without keys or hashes.

post.summary: POST /api/site/share-links: create a link and return its key once.

delete.summary: DELETE /api/site/share-links/{id}: revoke a link. Revoking twice is still 204.

post.summary:
Creates a station key in the caller's tenant. The caller may only hand out capabilities they
hold themselves, so managing stations is not a way to gain access.
Takes effect on the station's next request: the key is checked against the store every time.

get.summary: GET /api/tenants: list all tenants (platform admin).

post.summary: POST /api/tenants — create a tenant (platform admin).

get.description:
For a renderer serving several sites from one container, which has to know the tenant before it
can read anything else.
            
Anonymous, because that question is asked before anyone signs in, and it answers with the handle
and nothing more. Which tenant answers on a public domain is already public, since the domain
serves it; the rest of the tenant record is not.
            
It resolves the host the way request resolution does: a registered domain from the same cached
map first, then the leading subdomain. The map holds only active tenants, but the subdomain rule
names a handle without looking it up, so that branch checks the tenant exists and is active
before answering. Otherwise any made-up subdomain would come back as a handle.
get.summary: GET /api/tenants/by-host/{host}: the tenant a domain belongs to.

delete.summary: DELETE /api/tenants/external-role-map: removes the map. Roles already given stay.

get.summary: GET /api/tenants/external-role-map: the caller's tenant's claim-to-role map.

put.summary: PUT /api/tenants/external-role-map: sets the caller's tenant's map, replacing any.

get.summary: GET /api/tenants/members: the roster for the caller's tenant, newest first.

post.summary: POST /api/tenants/members: add a person to the caller's tenant by email.

get.summary: GET /api/tenants/members/roles: the roles an administrator may assign inside a tenant.

delete.summary: DELETE /api/tenants/members/{userId}: mark a member Removed in the caller's tenant.

put.summary: PUT /api/tenants/members/{userId}: change a member's roles, status or profile within the caller's tenant.

get.description:
The ask endpoint of Caddy's on-demand TLS, which sends the server name as domain and
issues a certificate only on a 200. It answers 200 for a domain an active tenant holds and 404 for
anything else, and says nothing about which tenant: by-host already answers that for a
mapped domain, and this one has no reason to.
            
Anonymous, because the proxy asks during a TLS handshake with nobody signed in. Only the cached
domain map is read, so a made-up name costs no query, and the tls-ask rate limit holds a
flood of them to 60 a minute per address. The leading-subdomain rule is not consulted: a tenant
reached as a subdomain of the deployment's own domain is covered by that domain's certificate,
and answering yes for any subdomain would let anyone have certificates issued for names nobody
registered.
get.summary: GET /api/tenants/tls-ask?domain={host}: whether a reverse proxy may get a certificate for a host.

POST /api/users/{userId}/password: an administrator holding manage_users sets another user's
password (recovery or rotation). Enforces the password policy and revokes the user's refresh
tokens; no current-password check, since this is an administrative reset. Outstanding
