get.description:
Gated on the capability that reads workflow runs rather than one of its own. A delivery row is
a run's action seen from the wire, and "did it fire?" is the same question as "did the run
succeed?" asked by the same person.
            
ResponseBody asks for more: a provider's response can echo
a credential (see Models/WebhookDelivery.cs), so reading it also needs
ViewWebhookResponseBodies. A caller holding only
ViewWorkflowRuns still gets every row, with the status, the
error and everything else the row carries; only the body itself is withheld. See issue #607.

parameters.description: A status class: 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx, or failed for no response at all.
parameters.name: status

get.summary: The delivery log, newest first.

parameters.description: The name of a RunStatus, in any case. Left out, every status is listed.
parameters.name: status

parameters.description: Only the runs of this workflow. Left out, every workflow's runs are listed.
parameters.name: workflowId

parameters.description:
A cursor from an earlier response, or a timestamp for the first call. Left out, the list is
newest first as before. Given, only runs changed after it are listed, oldest change first.
parameters.name: changedSince

post.description:
For a run nobody intends to finish, such as one whose halting action ended Unknown, or that
failed part way and has to be rolled back by hand. An action that succeeded and declares no
compensation is reported as not undone, and the run then reads Incomplete.
            
Refused while an action is in flight under a live lease, since the run cannot be undone around
a request that may still arrive; for a run already stopped, already rolled back, or finished
with every action succeeded; and for a workflow that is switched off or deleted, the same as a
retry, because a compensation is an action that goes out.
post.summary:
Gives up on a run and undoes what it did: what has not started is cancelled, and each action
that succeeded has its compensation run, the last first.

post.description:
Deliberately does not execute. Pressing retry queues the attempt and the runner picks it up, so
a slow provider cannot hold an HTTP request open and a retry behaves exactly like the original.
            
An action that already succeeded is refused: the whole reason a run records each action
separately is so that retrying a failed third one does not re-send the first two.
            
Retrying an action that halted its run is the resume: the actions its failure skipped are queued
again behind it, and run once it succeeds. One of those skipped actions is refused on its own,
since running it is running past the failure.
post.summary: Queues one action of a run to be attempted again.

post.description:
An action running under a live lease is left. Its request is already with the third party, so
it finishes and records its outcome, and the run ends after it. If it fails it is not queued
again. An action still marked running after its lease ran out becomes Unknown: it was claimed,
so it may have gone out, and Cancelled is kept for an action that never did.
            
The write is the same optimistic one the runner's claim makes on the run, so a cancel and a
claim of the same run cannot both be saved. Whichever is second is refused: the runner moves on,
and this answers 409 so the request can be sent again for what is left.
post.summary: Stops one run: every action that has not started is cancelled and nothing more is started.

get.summary: Endpoint to list all available workflow action plugins with metadata.

post.summary: Endpoint to test workflow execution without side effects (dry-run mode).

get.description:
Read with the runs, so it asks for view_workflow_runs. The window cannot reach past what
the retention sweep keeps: a longer one would divide the successes it kept by failures it did
not, and the response says the window it used.

parameters.description: How many days back the rate and the average look. Left out, seven. Clamped to what retention keeps.
parameters.name: windowDays

get.summary: GET /api/workflows/health. Each workflow's recent outcomes, success rate and action time, paged by workflow.

post.summary: Endpoint to validate workflow JSON schema.

get.summary: Endpoint to get available template variables for a content type.

delete.description:
Cancels and does not refuse. A workflow somebody wants gone is usually one that keeps failing,
and a failing workflow always has an attempt waiting on its backoff, so refusing while a run is
queued would refuse exactly the delete this exists for. Leaving the runs would not stop it
either: a run carries a copy of its actions and goes on without the definition.
            
The cancels, the delete and the audit entry are one transaction. A run the runner writes in
between refuses the whole of it, and the request is sent again.
delete.summary: Deletes one workflow, cancelling the runs it still has queued.

put.description:
A full update: every field the create takes is replaced, and a field left out takes the create's
default, so leaving out enabled switches the workflow on as it would a new one. The id is
the route's.
Credentials are write-only, so a caller holding a workflow read back from the API never has
them to send again. An action sent back unchanged, in the same position with the same type and
every shown parameter as the API returned it, keeps its stored credentials, its Conditional
children's included. A changed action that leaves a credential out is refused with a 400 naming
it: a credential stays with the destination it was given for. Sending one blank clears it, and
sending a value replaces it. A changed Conditional branch is taken as sent.
Runs already queued keep the copy of the actions they were queued with. The change applies to
runs queued from here on.
put.summary: Replaces one workflow with the definition sent, validated the way a create is.

get.summary: Endpoint to get workflow execution history for debugging.

put.description:
Its own endpoint because workflows have no update, and switching one off is the thing an
operator needs in a hurry: a workflow pointed at the wrong place fires on every publish until
somebody can stop it.
            
Off, the workflow starts no runs. Runs it had already queued are not touched here: the runner
cancels each one when it reaches it, so this request does not grow with the queue, and a run
queued a moment before the switch is caught the same way.
put.summary: Switches one workflow on or off.

post.description:
Queues and returns, like every other way a run starts: the runner does the work. The workflow's
conditions are checked and not bypassed. Having a run start past them is a different feature.
            
Reads Idempotency-Key itself. The run id is derived from the tenant, the caller, the
workflow, the entry and the key, so a repeat by the same caller finds the run, and the same key
on another workflow or entry, or from another caller, is another run. The repeat holds until
retention removes the run, not past it. The global idempotency filter would answer a key on
another workflow or entry with a 422, so it is told to leave this route alone.
            
An entry the caller cannot read is a 404, as an entry that does not exist is: the id of a hidden
entry should not be confirmable by trying to run something on it.
post.summary: POST /api/workflows/{id}/run. Starts one workflow on one entry, as a run with trigger Manual.

POST /ofrep/v1/evaluate/flags: every flag the caller may see, evaluated. Carries
an ETag, and answers 304 to a matching If-None-Match, so a client-side provider can poll cheaply.
POST /ofrep/v1/evaluate/flags/{key}: one flag, evaluated for the caller.
